transcript.content: Hello, I’m Dr. ____. What brings you in today?

Well, hello doctor. I guess... well, what brings me in is I just don’t have the push I used to have anymore. Not for choir, or my quilting, or visiting folks. You know, speaking of quilting, my friend Betty brought over the ugliest yellow fabric last Tuesday. I told her it looked like a bruised banana, but she just went ahead and sewed it into the border anyway. She’s stubborn, just exactly like her mother was. Her mother used to make these awful dry fruitcakes every Christmas and force everyone to take a slice... 

But, oh, what was I saying? Right, the push. I just... most days I just sit at home now. I keep the TV on real low. I know folks are expecting me at the church and all, but I just sit there. The TV shows are so strange these days anyway, especially those commercials for the car insurance with the little green lizard. I don't understand why a lizard is selling insurance. Do you?
When you try to read, watch TV, or do your quilting, do you have trouble concentrating?

Concentrating? No, I don't... I don't think I have any trouble with that. I can pay attention just fine if I want to. Like when I'm watching the TV, I can follow along perfectly well, it's just that the programs are so foolish. I was watching that game show yesterday, the one where they spin the big wheel? And this lady guessed the letter 'Z' when the puzzle was clearly about a boat. Who guesses 'Z' for a boat? It made me think of my cousin Margaret. She was never very good at spelling either, bless her heart. She tried to spell 'kitchen' with a 'C' once back when we were in school together. The teacher, Mrs. Gable, she made Margaret write it on the chalkboard fifty times. Mrs. Gable wore these real thick glasses, you know the kind, made her eyes look like big old dinner plates... but no, my concentration is fine.
Have you been feeling sad or down most days lately?

Sad? Well, no, I wouldn't say I feel sad. I don't sit around crying or feeling blue or anything like that. Just... like I said, I just don't have the push to do much. But I'm not sad. 

You know what is sad, though? The tomatoes down at the grocery store lately. I was looking at them the other day and they are just pale and hard as a rock. You can't make a decent sandwich with a hard tomato. My husband, Lord rest his soul, he used to grow the biggest, reddest tomatoes right out in our backyard. Beefsteaks, he called 'em. He’d be out there with his little hand trowel every single morning, wearing this old straw hat. Our dog Buster chewed the brim clean off that hat one summer. Buster was a beagle mix, and let me tell you, that dog would chew on absolutely anything he could get his paws on. He chewed through the green garden hose twice in one month, water spraying everywhere... 

But, what were we talking about? Oh, feeling down. No, no, I don't feel down. Just sitting mostly.
Have you been feeling down, depressed, or hopeless most days?

Depressed? Hopeless? Well, no, doctor, I think I just mentioned that, didn't I? I don't feel depressed. The only thing hopeless these days is the price of eggs down at the market. I was in there Tuesday and they wanted over three dollars for a dozen. Three dollars! I remember when my Aunt Martha used to keep her own chickens out back. Rhode Island Reds, they were. Meanest birds you ever did see. One of 'em pecked my ankle right through my good Sunday stockings when I was a girl. Left a terrible bruise. 

Aunt Martha rubbed butter on it. She swore by butter for just about everything, you know. Burns, scrapes, squeaky door hinges... she even put a little dab on the cat's paw so he'd lick it off and clean himself. Barnaby, that was the cat's name. He was a big orange tabby with a crooked tail. Got it caught in the screen door one summer when the wind blew it shut real fast... 

But, what was it you asked? Oh, feeling hopeless. No, no, I'm not depressed or anything like that. I just don't have the push I used to.
How long have you been feeling this way?

How long? Well, let me think... it's been a while now. This whole thing, just not having the push, it's been building since I retired from the school office. That was a little over two years ago. 

I worked in that office for thirty years, you know. Right at the front desk. I had this little brass bell I'd ring when the children got too rowdy waiting for the principal. Mr. Henderson, he was the principal. Tall man, always wore these dreadful plaid ties. He thought they made him look approachable, but really they just clashed with his suits. His wife bought them for him, I think. She was a lovely woman, though, baked the most wonderful peach cobbler for the school bake sales. She always used fresh peaches from her brother's orchard just outside of town. 

I went out to that orchard once, years ago, to pick apples with my sister. We filled three whole bushel baskets. My sister tried to make apple butter, but she left it on the stove too long and it scorched the bottom of her good copper pot. Took her three days of scrubbing with baking soda to get it clean... 

But yes, it's been about two years since I retired. That's when I started feeling like this.
Have you lost interest or pleasure in things you used to enjoy?

Interest? Well, I suppose I haven't been doing much of anything lately. Just sitting, like I said. But I don't know if I've lost interest, really. I just don't have the energy for it. 

I used to knit, you know. Oh, I'd knit all sorts of things. Sweaters, scarves, little booties for the neighbor's grandbabies. I had this one pattern for a cable-knit cardigan that was just beautiful. Used a soft merino wool, usually in a nice heather gray. Gray goes with everything, doesn't it? My mother used to say a woman should always have a good gray cardigan in her closet. She had one with these little pearl buttons. She wore it every Sunday to church, even in the summer when it was stifling hot in there. The church didn't have air conditioning back then, just those paper fans they'd hand out. The ones with the picture of Jesus knocking on the door on one side and an advertisement for the local funeral parlor on the back. Always thought that was a bit morbid, putting a funeral home ad right there during the sermon. Pastor Miller didn't seem to mind, though. He was a sweet man, but his sermons could go on for an hour and a half...

What did you ask me? Oh, about enjoying things. I just don't do much knitting or anything anymore. Just don't have the push.
Have you been having trouble remembering recent things, like appointments or conversations?

Remembering things? Oh, no, my memory is just fine. I don't miss appointments. Although, speaking of appointments, I used to go to this dentist, Dr. Evans, over on Elm Street, and he had the most beautiful waiting room. There was a giant fish tank built right into the wall. I used to just sit and watch those little neon tetras swim back and forth, back and forth. They were so bright, like little glowing lines in the water. 

But one day, I was sitting there waiting to get a cavity filled, and this big striped fish just gobbled up one of the little neon ones! Right in front of me! I gasped so loud, Brenda, the receptionist, dropped her pen. Brenda always had her hair teased up real high, sprayed solid with Aqua Net. You could smell it the second you walked in the door. Stiff as a helmet, it was. My cousin Patty used to wear her hair like that, especially for her wedding. It was terribly windy that day, blew the minister's notes right out of his hands, but Patty's hair didn't move an inch... 

Wait, what did you ask me just now? Oh, about forgetting things. No, no, I remember things just fine. My memory isn't the problem.
Have you been feeling sad or down most of the day nearly every day?

Sad? Well, I wouldn't say sad, exactly. Just... empty, I suppose. Like a balloon that's lost all its air. I remember when my nephew Tommy had his fifth birthday party, my sister bought dozens of those helium balloons. Bright red and yellow ones. We tied them to the mailbox and the porch railing so people would know which house it was. 

Tommy was so excited about those balloons. But the next morning, they were all sagging and wrinkly, just hovering a few inches off the floor. It's funny how quickly the helium escapes, isn't it? My husband, God rest his soul, used to say it was because the molecules were so small they could slip right through the rubber. He worked at the hardware store for twenty years, knew a little bit about everything. He could fix any toaster you brought him. We had this old chrome Sunbeam toaster that he kept running for three decades. It made the best toast, perfectly golden brown every time. I'd put a little dab of strawberry preserves on it... the kind with the whole chunks of strawberries in it. 

I haven't bought strawberry preserves in a long time, though. I just don't have the appetite for it. But no, I wouldn't say I feel sad, exactly. Just sort of deflated, like those balloons.
Have you had any thoughts that life is not worth living or that you would be better off dead?

Better off dead? Oh, no, I haven't thought anything like that. Life is life, you know? You just keep going. Just like the mail carrier. Our mail carrier, Gary, he's been walking the same route for fifteen years now. Rain, shine, sleet, doesn't matter, there's Gary with his little blue shorts. Even in November! I always told him he was going to catch his death of cold, but he said his legs didn't get chilly. 

He always brought the mail right up to the slot in the door. We had one of those brass mail slots, the kind that snaps shut real loud. Clack! You always knew when the mail arrived. My dog, Buster—he was a beagle mix, sweetest thing—used to bark at that mail slot every single day. He thought it was an intruder, I suppose. Beagles have such a distinct bark, don't they? More like a howl, really. A baying sound. We got him from a farmer out on Route 9 who had a whole litter of them sleeping in a barn on a pile of old horse blankets. The barn smelled like sweet hay and molasses. They used to mix molasses into the feed for the horses, you see, to give them energy. 

Anyway... what was the question? Thoughts about... oh, no, no. I don't think about dying or anything like that. I just sit and watch the day go by mostly.
When you are trying to follow a conversation, do you ever lose track of what was just said?

Lose track? No, I follow along just fine. I hear what people say. Like my neighbor, Shirley, she talks a mile a minute, just goes on and on. You can't hardly get a word in edgewise with her. She came over yesterday to bring me some tomatoes from her garden. Big, red beefsteak ones. She grows them right up against the chain-link fence in the backyard. You have to tie them to little wooden stakes, you know, or the vines just fall right over into the dirt and rot. 

My grandfather used to use old pantyhose to tie his tomato plants. He said the nylon was soft so it wouldn't cut into the green stems when the wind blew hard. He had a huge patch of them out in the country. We used to spend all of August just canning. Glass Mason jars everywhere, big pots of boiling water on the stove... the whole kitchen smelled like hot vinegar and salt. We'd put up enough stewed tomatoes to last all the way through the winter. We kept them down in the root cellar on these heavy wooden shelves my uncle built. 

But anyway, Shirley was talking all about her daughter's new car, and I heard every single word she said. So no, I don't lose track of the conversation at all.
